name: Elevating regional maternal and child health standards

content.text: The multi-partner, five-year CAHSS aims to strengthen healthcare systems in inaccessible areas of Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Afghanistan and Pakistan by imparting crucial knowledge and evidence-based clinical skills to professionals in maternal, newborn and child health (MNCH) and nutrition.

Speaking about the need for the CAHSS, Dr Sajid Soofi, Associate Professor in Paediatrics and Child Health, said "All four countries under the programme have large rural populations. The quality of medical facilities and practices in these inaccessible areas are far behind urban areas which leaves mothers exposed to undue risks during pregnancy.

"It also leaves their children vulnerable to threats from infections and complications during birth, and issues such as malnutrition and infectious diseases in their early years. Our intensive courses built the capacity of 107 healthcare practitioners enabling them to solve common problems around them and thereby improve the health of women and children in their communities."

Courses for each country were designed after AKU faculty visited local experts and healthcare institutions around each nation in order to assess gaps that were impeding service delivery. Faculty then designed the MNCH curriculum in line with World Health Organization guidelines before customising each country's curriculum to tackle its particular challenges.

For example courses conducted in Afghanistan and the Northern Areas of Pakistan had a greater emphasis on tackling anemia (a condition caused by a lack of red blood cells), micronutrient deficiencies, and the blood disorder, thalassemia. But in Tajikhistan and Kyrgyzstan, instructors focused on developing healthcare practices to tackle the threats of sexually-transmitted diseases and childhood obesity.

Dr Shabina Ariff, Assistant Professor in Paediatrics and Child Health, said that professionals welcomed the training since courses were conducted in the local language and because modern teaching methods including videos, mannequins and clinical case studies were used to pass on experience in managing diseases.

Highlighting the need for such educational programmes, Dr Ariff added that a lack of medical colleges and professional training courses in Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan meant that many professionals were not exposed to updated clinical skills that were routine in other parts of the world.

"Over 65 percent of health professionals in Tajikistan had not attended professional development courses for more than five years. We also noticed that many medical graduates could not access refresher training or continuing medical educational programmes which was impacting their ability to treat patients.

"Over the next two years we plan to double the number of students receiving the course so that 250 healthcare practitioners can apply the knowledge and skills imparted under our MNCH curriculum," Dr Ariff added.

Students on the weeklong, full-day courses welcomed the chance to refresh their skills and learn from best practices around the world. Many participants learnt resuscitation techniques for the first time and gained crucial information about measuring malnutrition and managing complications during pregnancy.
One participants from Kygyzstan said: "The sessions were great because we have a lot of cases with preterm birth and when I will go to Koshkor, I will share these learning with my colleagues."

The CAHSS project is aimed at strengthening service delivery, fostering professional and continuing education, reinforcing community health promotion, and promoting learning to improve the health indicators of Central Asia, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

The project is funded by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade Development, Canada, and is being implemented by the Aga Khan Foundation (AKF). The other AKDN bodies working with AKF are the Aga Khan Health Service and the French Medical Institute for Mothers and Children.
